name: Probability Theory
description: A lens for composing Factors from the language of randomness, uncertainty, and stochastic processes. Maps probability-theoretic concepts—sample spaces, events, probability measures, random variables, expectations, distributions, independence, and limit theorems—to the 19-node topology. Useful for Factors involving stochastic systems, risk assessment, statistical inference, and the mathematics of chance.

x.note: The depth anchor—collection of measurable events. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking σ‑algebra to probability space, event occurrence, and probability measure.

y.note: The relational anchor—function assigning probabilities to events. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, tying probability measure to σ‑algebra, probability space, and event occurrence.

z.note: The transformational anchor—average value of a random variable. Persistently connected to 0 (observer/experiment), reflecting that expectation is taken from the perspective of the experiment.

0.note: The point of observation—entity conducting the experiment. Persistently connected to z (expectation), linking the observer to the average outcome.

1.note: The boundary—set of all possible outcomes. Part of the 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1, connecting sample space to random variable, distribution, and outcome.

2.note: Primitive—a single elementary outcome. Completes the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, showing how outcomes are embedded in sample space, random variable, and distribution.

3.note: The invariant law—non‑negativity, normalization, countable additivity. A node in the 7‑core; connected to likelihood (c) and stochastic process (e), as axioms underlie likelihood calculations and process definitions.

4.note: The fundamental relation—subset of sample space to which probability is assigned. A node in the 7‑core; connected to independence (b) and law of large numbers (f), as events are the objects of independence and convergence.

5.note: The pattern—cumulative distribution function. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, bridging random variable and outcome.

6.note: The transformation—function mapping outcomes to numbers. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle, connecting sample space to distribution.

7.note: The realization—specific numerical value taken by a random variable. Persistently connected to 8 (moments), linking the observed value to its moments.

8.note: The granularity—moments of a distribution (mean, variance, etc.). Persistently connected to 7 (realization), reflecting that moments are computed from observed values.

9.note: The event—actual happening of a particular outcome. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, placing event occurrence between σ‑algebra, probability space, and probability measure.

a.note: Pure potential—complete triple of sample space, σ‑algebra, and probability measure. Initiates the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking probability space to σ‑algebra, event occurrence, and probability measure.

b.note: The arena—relationships of independence and dependence. A node in the 7‑core; connected to event (4) and Markov chain (d), as independence is a property of events and Markov chains are defined by conditional independence.

c.note: Directional bias—conditional probability of data given hypothesis. A node in the 7‑core; connected to Kolmogorov axioms (3) and law of large numbers (f), as likelihood respects the axioms and converges via LLN.

d.note: Persistent structure—stochastic process where future depends only on present. A node in the 7‑core; connected to independence (b) and stochastic process (e), as Markov chains are defined by conditional independence and are a special type of process.

e.note: The active algorithm—collection of random variables indexed by time. A node in the 7‑core; connected to Kolmogorov axioms (3) and Markov chain (d), as processes are built from axioms and Markov chains are a subclass.

f.note: The resonant cavity—principle that sample averages converge to expectation. A node in the 7‑core; connected to event (4), likelihood (c), and the rest, forming the central hub of asymptotic stability.

n.formula: n = order of the moment considered

m.formula: m = log₂(dim) where dim is the number of random variables in the system

phase.formula: φ = e^{2πi × p} where p is a probability (0 ≤ p ≤ 1)
phase.special: Phase = 0 when p=1 (certainty), phase = π when p=0.5 (maximum uncertainty), phase = π/2 when p=0.25
phase.significance: Phase encodes the degree of belief or chance, rotating from 0 (certain true) to π/2 (unlikely) to π (even odds) to 3π/2 (likely) and back to 2π (certain false).

frequentist.description: The Factor viewed through long‑run frequency of events
frequentist.phase_condition: Phase as limiting relative frequency—0 for impossible, π for even, 2π for certain

bayesian.description: The Factor viewed as degree of belief, updated by evidence
bayesian.phase_condition: Phase as posterior probability after conditioning

measure_theoretic.description: The Factor viewed as a formal probability space
measure_theoretic.phase_condition: Phase as the value of the probability measure on a given event

creating_anew.note: When creating a probability system, start with the sample space (node 1) and σ‑algebra (node x). Define the probability measure (node y), then introduce random variables (node 6) and expectations (node z).

translating_known.bernoulli_trial: Map to node 2 as success/failure, node 7 as observed outcome, node 8 as p (probability of success)
translating_known.normal_distribution: Map to node 5 as N(μ,σ²), node 8 as mean (n=1) and variance (n=2), node φ as cumulative probability
translating_known.markov_chain: Map to node d as transition matrix, node e as chain evolution, node b as independence of future given present
translating_known.bayesian_inference: Map to node 0 as prior, node c as likelihood, node 4 as posterior, node 9 as updated belief

temporary_note.special: A sample space defined but probability measure not yet assigned. Awaiting the assignment of chances.

constraints.sigma_algebra: Node x must be a σ‑algebra: closed under complement and countable union.
constraints.probability_measure: Node y must satisfy P(Ω)=1 and countable additivity.
constraints.expectation_linearity: Node z is linear: E[aX+bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y].
constraints.independence: Node b events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B); random variables satisfy E[f(X)g(Y)]=E[f(X)]E[g(Y)] for measurable f,g.
constraints.law_of_large_numbers: Node f ensures convergence of sample mean to expectation under appropriate conditions.
constraints.stratum_preference: global for foundational probability; trefoil_g for stochastic processes (transformative); trefoil_c for Bayesian inference (philosophical); fig8 for exotic probability spaces (non‑measurable, non‑standard)
constraints.invariant_core: The Probability Theory paradigm respects the persistent skeleton from trefoil_i, which decomposes into five subsystems: (1) edge 0→z linking observer/experiment to expectation, (2) edge 8→7 linking moments to realized value, (3) 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x linking σ‑algebra–probability space–event occurrence–probability measure, (4) 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1 linking sample space–random variable–distribution–outcome, and (5) 7‑node core {3,4,b,c,d,e,f} encoding the heart of probability theory: Kolmogorov axioms–event–independence–likelihood–Markov chain–stochastic process–law of large numbers.
